Section 1 of 9

Can the world ever be safe if cruelty never ends?

When people hurt others and escape responsibility, it can be hard to believe justice will come. When harm continues across generations, promises of a better future may feel far away.

In our last lesson, we explored God’s judgment. This lesson asks what comes afterward.

Will suffering continue somewhere forever? Does God enjoy punishing people? What does the Bible mean by the final destruction of evil?

These are serious questions. You are welcome to take your time with them.

God Wants People to Live

Read Ezekiel 33:11 ↗ and 2 Peter 3:9 ↗.

God says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. He calls people to turn from destructive ways and live. His patience gives people an opportunity to receive His mercy.

That matters when we read about judgment. The Creator loves the people He made, including those who have turned against Him.

He does not look for reasons to reject you. Through Jesus, He has acted to save you.

If religious threats have made you afraid to ask questions, remember this: honest questions are welcome here. Understanding God’s character takes more than being frightened into agreement.

What Does “Wicked” Mean?

Read Romans 3:23–24 ↗ and John 3:16–19 ↗.

The Bible teaches that all of us have sinned. Every person needs forgiveness and a changed heart.

“Wicked” is never a proper label for an ethnicity, language, hairstyle, or Native identity. No people are naturally closer to God than another.

In the final judgment, the issue is a person’s response to God and their persistent choice to hold on to evil. God knows each life fully, including the opportunities and understanding that person had.

Your ancestry does not place you outside His love. Neither does membership in a religious group make anyone automatically right with Him.

We all come to God through the same mercy.

Why Must Evil End?

Read Psalm 37:10–11 ↗ and Revelation 21:4 ↗.

Think about what a truly safe future would require.

People could live without fear of abuse. Families would no longer face violence. No one could gain power by humiliating or exploiting someone else.

For that future to last, evil must end.

God’s forgiveness offers people a way out of sin. But He will not allow those who permanently refuse that rescue to keep harming His creation forever.

His final judgment brings an end to rebellion and its suffering. The promise of peace includes the promise that cruelty will never return.

When Does This Happen?

Read Revelation 20:4–15 ↗.

Revelation describes a thousand-year period between two resurrections. Those who belong to Jesus live and reign with Him. The rest of the dead are raised afterward.

At the end of this period, Satan makes a final attempt to gather people against God’s beloved city. Fire from God consumes them. Judgment ends in what Revelation calls the “second death.”

This is the final destruction of evil. Satan will not rule an underground kingdom where he tortures people forever. He also faces judgment and destruction.

This lesson follows the understanding that God’s final judgment consumes evil and cleanses the earth, making way for a restored creation. Further reading on this understanding ↗.

Does Punishment Last Forever?

Read Romans 6:23 ↗, Matthew 10:28 ↗, and Malachi 4:1–3 ↗.

Romans describes the result of sin as death. Eternal life is God’s gift through Jesus.

Jesus speaks of God’s power to destroy both body and soul. Malachi pictures the final destruction as a fire that leaves neither root nor branch.

Together, these passages point to a final end of life for those who persistently reject God.

We understand the Bible to teach that the lost will face real judgment and punishment, ending in complete destruction. God will not keep them alive in endless suffering.

The second death is permanent. There is no later resurrection from it.

What About “Eternal Fire”?

Read Matthew 25:46 ↗ and Jude 7 ↗.

Some Bible passages are difficult. Matthew speaks of eternal punishment, and Jude describes the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of eternal fire.

Those cities are not still burning today. The fire’s destruction was lasting.

This helps explain our understanding of eternal punishment: its result lasts forever. It does not require an endless process of dying without ever reaching death.

Revelation 20:10 ↗ also uses the words “for ever and ever.” Readers understand this passage differently. We read its picture of judgment alongside Revelation’s description of the second death and the passages that describe the wicked being consumed.

You do not need to rush past a difficult verse. Read the passages together. Write down your questions. Careful discussion is part of learning.

Can We Trust God With People We Love?

Read Genesis 18:25 ↗ and Romans 2:11–16 ↗.

Perhaps this lesson brings someone to mind: a grandparent, a friend, or someone who was deeply hurt by religion.

You do not have to decide that person’s eternal future.

God knows what they understood, what they experienced, and how they responded to the light available to them. His judgment is impartial and fully informed.

We cannot see another person’s whole heart. We can trust that God will judge rightly.

Concern for someone you love can become a prayer. It does not have to become a burden of trying to take God’s place.

How Should This Change Our Lives Now?

Read Romans 12:19–21 ↗.

God’s coming judgment gives no one permission to threaten, shame, or harm another person.

It calls us to leave final judgment with Him while choosing what is right today. We can protect people, speak truth, seek accountability, and refuse revenge.

We can also receive the mercy we need ourselves.

Following Jesus begins with admitting that we need His help. We do not have to prove that we are better than someone else.

Read John 6:37 ↗.

Jesus welcomes those who come to Him. You can come with regret, uncertainty, and questions. You can ask Him to teach you how to live.

Think About It

  1. What have you heard about God’s final judgment? How has it affected your view of Him?
  2. What does Ezekiel 33:11 ↗ reveal about God’s heart?
  3. How does the promise that evil will end affect your understanding of a safe future?
  4. Which passage in this lesson would you like to discuss further?
  5. Is there someone whose future you need to entrust to God’s care?

Try This Over the Next Seven Days

Set aside a few quiet minutes each day. Read the passage and consider the question.

Day 1: Ezekiel 33:11 ↗. What does God want for people?

Day 2: John 3:16–17 ↗. What did God do to save us?

Day 3: Romans 6:23 ↗. How is eternal life received?

Day 4: Psalm 37:10–11 ↗. What would lasting peace look like?

Day 5: Revelation 20:11–15 ↗. What questions do I have about judgment?

Day 6: Romans 12:19–21 ↗. How can I respond to harm without seeking revenge?

Day 7: Revelation 21:1–5 ↗. What part of God’s promised future gives me hope?

A Prayer

Creator, some of these things are difficult to understand. Help me see Your justice and Your mercy together. Thank You for wanting people to live and for offering us forgiveness through Jesus. Help me turn from what harms others and myself. I place the people I love in Your care. Teach me to trust You and to bring my questions honestly. Amen.

Remember This

God takes no pleasure in anyone’s destruction. He offers forgiveness and life through Jesus.

His final judgment will bring evil to an end. Suffering will not continue forever.
